name: Hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids (CSF1R)
aliases: adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Typically presents in mid-adulthood with a combination of progressive cognitive decline, behavioural and personality change, and motor features such as parkinsonism, spasticity and gait disturbance
Caused by dominantly inherited mutations in the CSF1R gene, which encodes the colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor important for microglial function
MRI characteristically shows patchy, asymmetrical white matter change with frontal and periventricular predominance and involvement of the corpus callosum
Small foci of restricted diffusion that persist over time and punctate white matter calcification, best seen on CT or susceptibility-weighted imaging, are supportive clues
Seizures, apraxia and frontal-release signs may occur, and the phenotype is frequently mistaken for a primary psychiatric disorder or atypical dementia
A family history of early-onset dementia or leukoencephalopathy strengthens suspicion but many cases appear sporadic
Diagnosis is confirmed by CSF1R genetic testing, avoiding the need for brain biopsy in most patients
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids is an adult-onset white matter disorder caused by dominant mutations in CSF1R, which encodes a receptor essential for the survival and function of microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain. Impaired microglial signalling leads to a primary microgliopathy with secondary demyelination, axonal loss and the formation of swollen axonal spheroids together with pigmented glia within affected white matter. The frontal-predominant white matter degeneration underlies the characteristic combination of cognitive, behavioural and motor decline, and the disorder is grouped with adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia under the umbrella of CSF1R-related disease.
additionalDifferentials: Primary or metabolic leukodystrophies of adult onset
Vanishing white matter disease and other genetic leukoencephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted and susceptibility-weighted sequences to characterise the white matter pattern
CT of the head to detect punctate white matter calcification
CSF1R gene testing to confirm the diagnosis
Neuropsychological assessment to characterise the cognitive and behavioural profile
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help exclude inflammatory and infective causes
Metabolic and leukodystrophy screen to exclude alternative white matter disorders
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cognitive and motor decline in a relatively young adult
Recurrent seizures superimposed on a leukoencephalopathy
Behavioural change misattributed to a primary psychiatric illness delaying diagnosis
Family history of early-onset dementia raising genetic and counselling implications
reference.prognosis: The disorder is relentlessly progressive, with accumulating cognitive, behavioural and motor disability leading to dependency and reduced survival over a variable period of years; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, and genetic counselling is important for at-risk relatives.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as a primary psychiatric disorder or as multiple sclerosis
Overlooking the diagnostic value of persistent restricted diffusion foci and white matter calcification
Failing to offer genetic testing and counselling once a leukoencephalopathy pattern is recognised
Assuming an absent family history excludes a CSF1R mutation
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No established disease-modifying drug therapy; allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is under investigation as a means of replacing CSF1R-deficient microglia and stabilising progression in selected early cases
Symptomatic treatment of motor features with antispasticity agents for spasticity, dopaminergic trials for parkinsonism, and anticonvulsants for seizures
Management of cognitive and behavioural or psychiatric symptoms with judicious psychotropic support, avoiding the mistreatment that follows misdiagnosis as a primary psychiatric disorder
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and swallow assessment to address gait, function and aspiration risk
Advance care planning, carer support and coordinated management of progressive dependency
Genetic counselling and predictive testing for at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
